content_voiceover: This slide continues the same Taiwan chronic myeloid leukemia study, now breaking down cumulative incidence of specific molecular response milestones over time, again comparing children in blue to adults in red. Panel A shows the cumulative incidence of reaching an international scale below 1 percent, an early response milestone. At 5 years, 75 percent of adults reach this compared to only 58 percent of children, a significant difference. Panel B shows major molecular response, roughly a 3-log reduction. At 5 years, 66 percent of adults achieve this versus 48 percent of children. Panel C shows a deeper molecular response at the 4-log level, called MR4.0. Adults reach 44 percent at 5 years and 60 percent by 8 years, while children lag at 25 percent by 5 years and 41 percent by 8 years. Panel D shows an even deeper response at the 4.5-log level, MR4.5, sometimes considered a threshold for treatment discontinuation trials. Adults reach 34 percent at 5 years and 44 percent by 10 years, while children reach only 16 percent at 5 years and 32 percent by 10 years. Every single panel shows the same consistent pattern, children take longer to reach each milestone than adults, though the gap does narrow somewhat with more years of therapy.
keypoints: Children consistently reach IS less than 1%, MMR, MR4.0, and MR4.5 milestones later than adults on front-line imatinib
At 5 years, only 58% of children versus 75% of adults reach IS less than 1%
Deep molecular response thresholds like MR4.5, relevant to treatment-free remission trials, are reached by far fewer children at 5 years, 16% versus 34% in adults
Gap between children and adults narrows somewhat with longer follow-up but persists across all response depths
keypoint_voiceover: For exam purposes, remember that pediatric CML patients lag behind adults at every depth of molecular response on imatinib, from early IS less than 1 percent through deep MR4.5 responses relevant to stopping therapy trials. This slower kinetics is a normal feature of pediatric CML biology, not necessarily a sign of resistance or need to escalate therapy.
